prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the continuous ground plane sloping upward from bright near-field pavement (~1–2 m ahead at the bottom edge) to darker mid- and far-field grass, trees, and a white fence on the left (~15–25 m away), with no people present in the scene. Across the five frames, as the camera wearer moves forward and curves slightly left along the path, near-field vertical structures pop out brightly against the background: a lamppost on the left in frame 1 (~2–3 m away), a thin signpost on the right in frame 3 (~2–3 m away, just outside arm's reach), and a picnic table on the right in frames 4–5 that brightens as its distance shrinks from ~5–6 m to ~2.5–3.5 m beside a tree trunk (~3–5 m to the left) and bushes (~5–7 m behind the table). Unlike the RGB image where harsh tree shadows in frames 4 and 5 obscure the path and grass, the depth map provides a clean, illumination-invariant geometry of the ground surface and clearly separates the foreground lamppost, signpost, tree trunk, and picnic table from the background foliage. However, the depth map is unreliable for fine background structures, completely losing the distant playground equipment (~15–30 m ahead) and the houses beyond the left fence into uniform black sky/background, and failing to resolve the thin signpost in frame 1 (~12–15 m away) until the wearer gets closer in frames 2 and 3.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map is entirely blank in frames 1 through 3 and detects only the picnic table on the right side of the path in frames 4 and 5 (as the wearer approaches from ~5–6 m to ~2.5–3.5 m), confirming that no people or wearable-reach objects (<1 m) are detected in the scene. In frames 4 and 5, it splits the single picnic table into two separate 'bench' instances—one mask covering the tabletop and left/main frame, and a second mask covering the attached right-side seat bench (~0.5 m apart from each other, resting on the concrete pad below eye level). While this highlights the table's silhouette in frame 4 despite the dark tree shadow that reduces contrast in the RGB image, it provides almost no broader spatial layout compared to RGB or depth. The map is highly unreliable across the sequence: it misses the picnic table completely when it is ~8–20 m away in frames 1–3, fails to detect the nearby park bench under the tree (~8–10 m ahead in frames 4–5), and provides no masks for the lamppost, signpost, trees, fence, playground, or gazebo.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is completely black across all five frames, containing no yellow body keypoints or magenta hand skeletons. This supports the spatial fact visible in the RGB strip that no other people are present in the park—neither nearby nor in the distant playground (~15–35 m away) or gazebo (~12–25 m away)—so there are no human facing directions, gaze targets, or other people's reach zones to track. It also shows that the camera wearer's own hands and arms remain out of the camera's field of view (below or behind the lens) throughout the forward walk, with nothing held or manipulated within arm's reach in front of the camera. Because the scene contains only static park infrastructure and vegetation, the pose map contributes no environmental layout information and cannot aid in judging obstacle distances or occlusions.
